title: Bryce Harper addresses Cameo video sent by FanDuel to gambler: ‘I did not consent to it’
content:
Philadelphia Phillies star Bryce Harper says he was hoodwinked into filming a personalized video message for a gambling addict.

In a statement released Monday on his Instagram account, ahead of All-Star media availability and his Home Run Derby appearance, Harper offered his first comment on his appearance in a 21-second video to a FanDuel customer in November 2024. The video, which was first reported by the Philadelphia Inquirer on Thursday, was branded with the betting giant’s logo and showed Harper wishing a fan a happy Thanksgiving.

The fan, Terry Thompson, and another plaintiff are suing several sportsbooks, including FanDuel, claiming they use their products and VIP services to intentionally coerce bettors into gambling more. Thompson, who had VIP status with FanDuel, claims in the lawsuit that even as he incurred more than $1.5 million in gambling debt, his FanDuel VIP manager, Bryttanni Morgan, offered perks — like free tickets and hotel accommodations to attend the Super Bowl — and micro-bets to keep him gambling.

Harper’s name did not appear in the lawsuit. The video appears to be another perk Morgan procured for Thompson, a Philadelphia sports fan.

“What happened here went beyond anything I knew about or approved,” Harper said in the statement.

The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board is reviewing the video, according to ESPN.

Harper said he has no affiliation with FanDuel, which is an official betting partner of Major League Baseball. He claimed he had no knowledge that the video would be used for commercial purposes.

Harper explained that in November 2024 he received a video request on Cameo — a platform commonly used by athletes and celebrities to film personalized videos for paying fans — from someone identified as “Bryttanni.”

In a screenshot Harper shared, the request came with a brief script: “Hey Terry, Your host Bryttanni (Britt-knee) from FanDuel wanted to make sure your Thanksgiving was extra special, so I just wanted to hop on and wish you and your family a wonderful Thanksgiving. Tell Max (son) I said hello!” The submission suggested Harper could add “personal touches” to the message.

Harper followed that script in the video, then ended by thanking the recipient for his support and wishing him a happy holiday.

“I read (the script) in good faith,” Harper said in the statement. “FanDuel then put its own logo on the video and used it as a gambling promotion. I did not know FanDuel would do this, I did not consent to it, and FanDuel had no right to do it.

“Had I known FanDuel’s true intent, I would not have made the video. The same is true had I known anything about Terry or his situation, or about any alleged ‘partnership’ between Cameo and FanDuel.”

A recent report from Front Office Sports confirmed that FanDuel and Cameo have a partnership that permits Cameo videos to be purchased for FanDuel VIP bettors.

Harper contended that he believed at the time this was a personal request on Cameo.

“Cameo had a separate category for business video requests, and at the time I did not know this video would be used for commercial purposes,” Harper said in the statement.

Harper, who has made more than $250 million in his career, has rates beginning at $899 to purchase personal messages, according to his Cameo page. This instance raises questions about how Harper vets those requests and how Cameo communicates requests from partners such as FanDuel.

Harper could pursue litigation against FanDuel, according to two people briefed on the matter, who were granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly.

— The Athletic’s Matt Gelb contributed to this story.
